This page gets you from a fresh checkout to a **running local KMS** and the
**attestation-verifier** web app, then walks one `challenge → get-key` cycle
against your local instance. It is the fastest way to see the moving parts
before you read the flows in depth.

The production KMS only releases keys to nodes running inside a real Intel TDX
confidential VM, with [quotes signed by the hardware](/flows/attestation-flow/)
and keys derived from a cluster root that exists only inside TDX replicas. None
of that exists on a laptop, so the KMS ships a **dev-only mock path** (a Cargo
feature, off by default) that lets you run a single replica and exercise the
HTTP surface and most of the verification pipeline without TDX hardware.

:::caution
Everything on this page uses the mock-attestation build and mock acceptance.
That code is compiled out of the production binary and must **never** be used to
release real keys. See the [trust model](/understand/trust-model/) for why.
:::

## Prerequisites

- **Rust** 1.88+ (`rustup`, `cargo`) — the KMS is a Cargo workspace.
- **Node.js** 18+ and **npm** — for the attestation-verifier web app.
- `curl` and (optionally) `jq` — to drive the endpoints by hand.

## Build the KMS

The workspace has a single member, `mero-kms`. From the repository root:

```bash
# Debug build of the whole workspace
cargo build

# Or an optimized build
cargo build --release
```

This produces the production binary — it contains **no** mock-attestation code.
To run locally you want the dev build described next.

## Run the KMS in dev mode

Two independent things stand between a fresh start and a working `/get-key`
locally, and you have to satisfy both:

1. **Mock attestation** — accept mock TDX quotes instead of requiring real
   hardware-signed ones. This is gated behind the default-off `mock-attestation`
   Cargo feature, and only then is the `ACCEPT_MOCK_ATTESTATION` env var read.
2. **A cluster root** — `/challenge` and `/get-key` are fail-closed. Until the
   replica holds a root it returns `503 policy_not_ready`. Locally, make your
   single replica the bootstrap one with `MERO_KMS_BOOTSTRAP=true`, so it
   generates a root at startup instead of trying to join peers.

Build **with the feature** and set both knobs:

```bash
cd mero-kms
ACCEPT_MOCK_ATTESTATION=true \
MERO_KMS_BOOTSTRAP=true \
  cargo run --features mock-attestation
```

In mock mode the replica's own quote is a mock too, so the debug-TD and
RTMR3 startup checks that a real replica enforces are skipped.

:::caution
The `mero-kms` README shows `ACCEPT_MOCK_ATTESTATION=true cargo run`. Without
`--features mock-attestation` the flag is **silently ignored** — the mock path
is not compiled in — and mock quotes are rejected as unparseable. Always pass
`--features mock-attestation` for local dev.
:::

On startup the service logs its resolved configuration. Expect to see the mock
warning, the bootstrap flag, the `locked-read-only` profile, and the new root:

```text
INFO Starting mero-kms
INFO Listen address: 0.0.0.0:8080
INFO Cluster: bootstrap=true peers=[]
INFO KMS profile cohort: locked-read-only
WARN WARNING: Mock attestation acceptance is enabled. This should NEVER be used in production!
INFO Generated a new cluster root; this replica bootstraps the cluster
INFO Server listening on 0.0.0.0:8080
```

:::note
With mock acceptance on, the startup policy check is short-circuited, so the
replica starts even with empty `ALLOWED_*` allowlists — mock quotes skip the
measurement-policy comparison anyway. In a real image those lists are baked in
from the node release. If you want to exercise real measurement checks, set the allowlists:
`ALLOWED_TCB_STATUSES` (default `uptodate`) and `ALLOWED_MRTD`,
`ALLOWED_RTMR0`…`ALLOWED_RTMR3` (each a 96-hex-char TDX register value). See the
[configuration reference](/operate/config-reference/) for every variable and its
default.
:::

### Change the listen address (optional)

The HTTP listener defaults to `0.0.0.0:8080`. Override with `LISTEN_ADDR` if
`8080` is taken:

```bash
LISTEN_ADDR=127.0.0.1:9090 \
ACCEPT_MOCK_ATTESTATION=true \
MERO_KMS_BOOTSTRAP=true \
  cargo run --features mock-attestation
```

## Confirm it is up

`/health` is a liveness probe — it answers `200` whether or not the replica
holds a root, and says which:

```bash
curl -s http://localhost:8080/health
# {"status":"alive","service":"mero-kms","clusterRootReady":true}
```

## Walk one challenge → get-key cycle

Key release is a two-round challenge-response. Round 1 (`/challenge`) is fully
self-contained and works locally; round 2 (`/get-key`) runs the whole
verification pipeline and is where the local/hardware boundary shows up. Both
routes are documented in full in [Key Release](/flows/key-release/).

### Round 1 — get a challenge

Send any base58btc peer ID. The KMS mints a single-use nonce and returns a
stateless challenge ID (144 hex characters: the nonce, the expiry and an HMAC
tag under a root-derived key) plus the base64 nonce and its expiry:

```bash
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8080/challenge \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"peerId":"12D3KooWEyoppNCUx8Yx66oV9fJnriXwCcXwDDUA2kj6vnc6iDEp"}'
```

```json
{
  "challengeId": "<144 hex chars>",
  "nonceB64": "aGVsbG8td29ybGQtZXhhbXBsZS0zMi1ieXRlcy1ub25jZQ==",
  "expiresAt": 1753104000
}
```

The challenge is valid for `CHALLENGE_TTL_SECS` (default 60) and a replica
redeems it at most once.

### Round 2 — redeem it at /get-key

`/get-key` takes the challenge ID plus a TDX quote, the peer's public key, and a
signature binding all of it to the peer identity:

```bash
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8080/get-key \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "challengeId": "<144 hex chars from round 1>",
    "quoteB64":    "<base64 raw TDX quote with the nonce in report_data>",
    "peerId":      "12D3KooWEyoppNCUx8Yx66oV9fJnriXwCcXwDDUA2kj6vnc6iDEp",
    "peerPublicKeyB64": "<base64 protobuf libp2p public key>",
    "signatureB64":     "<base64 signature over the canonical payload>",
    "sealToB64":        "<base64 one-time X25519 public key>"
  }'
```

The KMS then, in order: validates the shapes, **redeems the challenge**
(so a replay to the same replica always fails on the second try), verifies the
peer signature and public-key ownership, verifies the quote (mock quotes are
accepted here in dev), enforces the measurement policy (skipped for accepted
mocks), and finally derives the key by HKDF from the root and seals it to
`sealToB64`. On success it returns:

```json
{ "sealedKeyB64": "<sealed storage key>", "sealNonceB64": "<12-byte nonce>" }
```

:::note
**What actually completes locally.** `/challenge` succeeds outright, and key
derivation needs no hardware now that it comes from the in-memory root.
Producing a valid mock `quoteB64` and the matching peer signature is still the
job of a real `merod` node (or the mock helpers in `calimero-tee-attestation`),
not a hand-written curl body — so treat round 2 as a structural walkthrough
unless you have a node in the loop.
:::

You can still observe the fail-closed behavior directly. Send a `/get-key`
request with placeholder credentials and watch the gates reject it, and watch
the challenge get redeemed even on failure:

```bash
# Second identical request returns invalid_challenge — the first attempt
# already redeemed the single-use challenge, regardless of why it failed.
```

Every error is a machine-readable tag with an HTTP status; the full catalog is
in [Error handling](/operate/error-handling/).

## Run the attestation verifier

The verifier is a separate React/Vite app with a serverless `/api/verify`
backend. Run it locally:

```bash
cd attestation-verifier
npm install
npm run dev
```

Vite serves it at `http://localhost:5173`. The two routes are `/kms` (verify a
pasted mero-kms `/attest` response; KMS replicas listen only inside their VPC)
and `/mero-tee` (verify a merod node by URL); the landing page redirects to
`/kms`.

:::note
The live verification path calls **Intel Trust Authority** and needs an
`ITA_API_KEY` in the environment — without it `/api/verify` returns
`503 ITA_API_KEY not configured`. The dev server also does not run the
serverless functions the way the production host does, so end-to-end
verification is best exercised against the deployed verifier. See
[Verify a release](/build/verify-a-release/) for the full UI walkthrough, and
[Verification](/flows/verification/) for what the checks mean.
:::
